title: Stern-Gerlach Experiment
short_intro: The Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrated the spatial quantization of angular momentum by passing a beam of silver atoms through an inhomogeneous magnetic field. It provided direct experimental evidence for electron spin and space quantization.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of the deflection of atomic beams, spatial quantization, and the concept of electron spin with two possible orientations.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed mathematical derivation of the magnetic force on a magnetic dipole, calculation of splitting in inhomogeneous fields, Hamiltonian of the interaction, and Larmor precession.

prerequisites: Electron spin and magnetic dipole moment

concept_notes.heading: Historical Context and Setup
bullets: Conducted by Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach in 1922 in Frankfurt, Germany.
Utilized an atomic beam of silver (Ag) atoms evaporated from an electrically heated oven in a high vacuum.
The beam passed through a specially shaped inhomogeneous magnetic field created by an asymmetric pole piece.

concept_notes.heading: Role of Inhomogeneous Magnetic Field
bullets: A uniform magnetic field exerts a torque on a magnetic dipole but no net translational force.
An inhomogeneous magnetic field exerts a net translational force proportional to the spatial derivative of the field component along the dipole axis.
The force is given by F_z = mu_z (d B_z / d z), which splits the beam into distinct spatial traces.

concept_notes.heading: Observation and Spatial Quantization
bullets: Classical physics predicts a continuous smearing or a broad single band on the detector plate corresponding to random orientations of magnetic moments.
The experiment observed the beam splitting into two discrete traces, proving that the magnetic moment component along the field can only take specific quantized values.
For silver atoms, the ground state has total orbital angular momentum L = 0, meaning the observed splitting is entirely due to the intrinsic spin angular momentum (S = 1/2) of the valence electron.

concept_notes.heading: Implications for Quantum Mechanics
bullets: Confirmed the space quantization rule where the z-component of angular momentum is m_s hbar, with m_s = +/- 1/2 for an electron.
Laid the foundation for modern magnetic resonance techniques and established spin as an inherent quantum degree of freedom.
Directly influenced the formulation of Pauli's exclusion principle and matrix mechanics.

derivations.title: Force on a Magnetic Dipole in an Inhomogeneous Magnetic Field
derivations.conditions: Magnetic dipole placed in a magnetic field pointing predominantly along the z-axis with a spatial gradient along z.

derivations.title: Deflection of Atomic Beam in Stern-Gerlach Apparatus
derivations.conditions: Silver atoms of mass m and velocity v passing through a magnetic field of length L with gradient d B_z / d z.
steps: Write the potential energy of the magnetic dipole in the field: U = - mu \cdot B = - mu_z B_z.
Determine the force along the z-direction: F_z = - (d U / d z) = mu_z (d B_z / d z).
Calculate the acceleration experienced by the atom: a_z = F_z / M = \frac{\mu_z}{M} \frac{d B_z}{d z}.
Determine the time spent in the magnetic field of length L: t = L / v.
Calculate the spatial deflection d along the z-axis on the detector: d = \frac{1}{2} a_z t^2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{\mu_z}{M} \frac{d B_z}{d z} \left(\frac{L}{v}\right)^2.

formula_sheet.name: Magnetic Moment of Electron Spin
formula_sheet.variables: mu_s = spin magnetic moment, g_s = gyromagnetic ratio (~2), e = electronic charge, m_e = electron mass, S = spin angular momentum

formula_sheet.name: Z-component of Spin Magnetic Moment
formula_sheet.variables: mu_sz = z-component of spin magnetic moment, mu_B = Bohr magneton

formula_sheet.name: Bohr Magneton
formula_sheet.variables: e = elementary charge, hbar = reduced Planck's constant, m_e = mass of electron

formula_sheet.name: Force on Magnetic Dipole
formula_sheet.variables: F_z = force in z direction, mu_z = magnetic moment component, d B_z / d z = magnetic field gradient

formula_sheet.name: Spatial Quantization Condition
formula_sheet.variables: J_z = z-component of total angular momentum, m_j = magnetic quantum number

formula_sheet.name: Potential Energy in Magnetic Field
formula_sheet.variables: U = potential energy, mu_z = magnetic moment component, B_z = magnetic field

formula_sheet.name: Number of Beam Components
formula_sheet.variables: N = number of split components, j = total angular momentum quantum number
formula_sheet.conditions: Space quantization rule for half-integer or integer spin

formula_sheet.name: Deflection Distance
formula_sheet.equation_html: z = \frac{\mu_z L^2}{2 m v^2} \frac{d B_z}{d z}
formula_sheet.variables: z = vertical deflection, L = length of field, m = atomic mass, v = velocity

graphs_and_experiments.title: Stern-Gerlach Experimental Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An oven emitting silver atoms, a collimating slit, an inhomogeneous magnet with wedge-shaped and flat pole pieces, and a detector plate showing two split traces.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how the atomic beam splits symmetrically into two discrete beams corresponding to m_s = +1/2 and m_s = -1/2.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in descriptive questions to identify components and explain the necessity of the inhomogeneous field.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Detector Plate Pattern (Classical vs. Quantum)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Comparison of expected continuous vertical smear (classical prediction) versus two distinct parallel lines (quantum observation).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Contrasts classical physics expectation of continuous orientation with quantum mechanics reality of discrete spatial quantization.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in objective questions to distinguish between classical and quantum mechanical outcomes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Sequential Stern-Gerlach Filters
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Three apparatuses in series: SG_z (selects +z), SG_x (selects +x), and a second SG_z.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates quantum measurement collapse, showing that measuring spin along x destroys the previously determined z-component information.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Advanced conceptual PGT questions on quantum state superposition and measurement.

solved_numericals.question: A beam of silver atoms passes through a Stern-Gerlach apparatus. How many traces are observed on the detector plate, and what does this indicate about the total angular momentum of the silver atom in its ground state?
solution_steps: Recall the formula for the number of split components: N = 2j + 1.
For silver atoms in the ground state, the valence electron is in the 5s orbital, so orbital angular momentum L = 0 and total spin S = 1/2.
solved_numericals.answer: 2 traces; indicates total angular momentum j = 1/2 (due to electron spin).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the force acting on a silver atom in a Stern-Gerlach magnet if the magnetic field gradient (d B_z / d z) is 1.5 x 1-^1 T/m. Assume the magnetic moment of the silver atom is equal to one Bohr magneton (mu_B = 9.27 x 10^-24 J/T).
solution_steps: Identify the formula for force on a magnetic dipole: F_z = mu_z (d B_z / d z).
Substitute the value of the magnetic moment mu_z = mu_B = 9.27 x 10^-24 J/T.
Substitute the field gradient d B_z / d z = 1.5 x 1^1 T/m.
Compute the product: F_z = (9.27 x 10^-24) x (1.5 x 1^1) = 1.39 x 10^-11 N.

solved_numericals.question: Find the vertical deflection of a silver atom (mass m = 1.79 x 10^-25 kg) passing through an inhomogeneous magnetic field of length L = 5.0 cm with a gradient of 1.0 x 1^2 T/m. Assume the atomic velocity is 500 m/s and mu_z = 9.27 x 10^-24 J/T.
solution_steps: Use the deflection formula: z = \frac{\mu_z L^2}{2 m v^2} \frac{d B_z}{d z}.
Substitute the given values: mu_z = 9.27 x 10^-24 J/T, L = 0.05 m, m = 1.79 x 10^-25 kg, v = 500 m/s, d B_z / d z = 1.0 x 1^2 T/m.
Final division: z approx 2.59 x 10^-5 m.

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the atomic beam is well-collimated and atoms do not interact with one another inside the beam (ideal gas approximation).
Neglects relativistic corrections to electron spin magnetic moment.
Valid only when the external magnetic field gradient is strong enough to overcome internal coupling effects (Paschen-Back regime relative to fine structure).

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Stern-Gerlach experiment proves the orbital angular momentum of electrons is quantized.
common_misconceptions.correct: In silver atoms, the orbital angular momentum is zero (L = 0), so the experiment specifically proves the quantization of electron spin.
common_misconceptions.why: Silver ground state has a single valence electron in an s-orbital, possessing no orbital angular momentum.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A uniform magnetic field is required to split the atomic beam.
common_misconceptions.correct: An inhomogeneous (non-uniform) magnetic field is strictly necessary to exert a translational force on the magnetic dipole.
common_misconceptions.why: A uniform field exerts only a torque, causing precession without translational deflection.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Classical mechanics can explain the two discrete spots on the detector.
common_misconceptions.correct: Classical physics predicts a continuous continuous band due to random dipole orientations.
common_misconceptions.why: Discrete splitting is a purely quantum mechanical manifestation of spatial quantization.

quick_revision: The Stern-Gerlach experiment verified space quantization and electron spin using a beam of silver atoms in an inhomogeneous magnetic field.
Magnetic Moment of Electron Spin: \mu_s = - g_s \frac{e}{2 m_e} S
